Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity

Zhuofan Josh Ying Affiliation: Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute; Columbia University, New York, NY Email: zy2559@columbia.edu    Peter Hase Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, CA Affiliation: Schmidt Sciences, New York, NY Email: phase@stanford.edu    Nikolaus Kriegeskorte Affiliation: Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute; Columbia University, New York, NY Email: nk2765@columbia.edu    Departments of Psychology    Neuroscience    Electrical Engineering
Abstract

Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report that a probe’s MCS to a reference probe trained on the out-of-distribution (OOD) data near-perfectly linearly predicts the probe’s OOD AUROC (R2=0.98R^{2}{=}0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove this general phenomenon in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe’s signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

1 Introduction

Linear probes are powerful interpretability tools (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Belinkov, 2022; Marks and Tegmark, 2023), but their transfer behavior is notoriously brittle: they often fail to generalize to closely related datasets, and break dramatically under subtle shifts such as negation or prompt-format changes (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Levinstein and Herrmann, 2024; Orgad et al., 2025). Understanding which probes generalize, and why two probes that look similar on one distribution diverge on another, requires a principled way to compare them.

Ying et al. (2026) report that the Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between a probe widw_{\mathrm{id}} trained on an in-distribution (ID) task and another probe woodw_{\mathrm{ood}} trained on an out-of-distribution (OOD) task, which reweights the inner product between the two probes by the OOD data covariance, is linearly related to the OOD AUROC of probe widw_{\mathrm{id}} (R2=0.98R^{2}{=}0.98). However, this was shown only for one model on truthfulness datasets, and such near-perfect linearity demands a theoretical explanation.

Empirically, we replicate and substantially extend this regularity. The near-linear AUROC–MCS relationship holds across models (Llama-70B, Llama-8B, Qwen-7B), across layers (20–65 of Llama-70B), and across 24 datasets from three concept domains (truthfulness, gender classification, and general NLP benchmarks), with R2>0.93R^{2}{>}0.93 in every condition. Euclidean cosine similarity (ECS), by contrast, drops to as low as R2=0.06R^{2}{=}0.06 (§2). Intuitively, ECS treats all dimensions equally, but only the dimensions where the data varies affect probe performance. MCS reweights the inner product by OOD data covariance, thus comparing probes in the subspace that actually matters.

Theoretically, we prove why this linear relationship holds. Under balanced classes and per-class projection Gaussianity, both the ID probe’s OOD AUROC and its MCS to the OOD probe are S-shapedd functions of the ID probe’s signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ss on the OOD task: AUROC is the Gaussian CDF Φ⁡(s/2)\Phi(s/\sqrt{2}) in ss, and MCS is a softsign function that converges to s/(4+s2)s/\sqrt{(4+s^{2})} with moderately large Fisher distance zmaxz_{\max}. Composing the two, where each S-shaped inverts the other’s curvature, cancels out the S-shapeds, leaving a near-linear AUROC–MCS curve (§3). The theory also predicts when the linearity fails: small zmaxz_{\max}, class imbalance, non-Fisher reference directions like difference of means, or using pooled covariance instead of the total covariance. We verify each failure mode in simulations or on real activations (§4).

Most elements here are textbook (Fisher, 1936; Green et al., 1966; Chatfield, 2018), and MCS itself is not new (Bolme et al., 2003; Iacovacci et al., 2020). The closest theoretical neighbor is Agreement-on-the-Line (Miller et al., 2021; Baek et al., 2022; Baek et al., 2025), which uses the same covariance-projected cosine to predict accuracy linearity between classifiers. Composing these ingredients into a closed-form law relating MCS and OOD AUROC is novel. See App. A for extended related works.

Together, MCS offers a theoretically grounded task-aware alternative for comparing linear probes.

2 Empirical evidence

Design.

We use Llama-3.3-70B at residual-stream layer 33, with mean-pooled activations over response tokens following Ying et al. (2026). To test generality, we additionally evaluate at layers {20,50,65}\{20,50,65\} of Llama-3.3-70B, at middle layers of Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B Qwen et al. (2025); Grattafiori et al. (2024). We use datasets across three domains exhibiting rich generalization patterns: ten truthfulness datasets, six gender classification datasets, and eight general NLP classification datasets. See App. B for details.

We train logistic-regression probes for each task. We denote the ID and OOD trained probe direction by widw_{\mathrm{id}} and woodw_{\mathrm{ood}}. For directions u,vu,v we define

MCSM⁡(u,v)≔u⊤​M​vu⊤​M​u​v⊤​M​v,\MC_{M}(u,v)\coloneqq\frac{u^{\top}Mv}{\sqrt{u^{\top}Mu}\sqrt{v^{\top}Mv}}, (1)

and instantiate MM with the full sample OOD train data covariance Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}.11 1 This is the opposite of the weighting in Mahalanobis distance (with Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}), which measures distances between points. Since we instead care about distances between probe weights (dual space) rather than data points (primal space), our formulation transforms data and probes inversely and thus preserves projections onto the probe in the whitened space as desired. We contrast against the pooled within-class covariance Σpool\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}} in §4. For each (ID, OOD) pair, we split the OOD data in half: on the train half, we train the probes and compute Σpool\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}, Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}, δ\delta, woodw_{\mathrm{ood}}, and SNR; on the disjoint test half, we compute the empirical AUROC of widw_{\mathrm{id}}. This avoids bias caused by overfitting.

Results.

We show that the OOD AUROC of widw_{\mathrm{id}} is a near-linear function of MCSΣtot⁡(wid,wood)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}), with R2≥0.93R^{2}{\geq}0.93 for all conditions tested (Fig. 1a, Tab. 1). ECS is substantially worse: R2R^{2} drops to 0.06 in the worst condition. Fig. 1b–c shows that the structure of the generalization-AUROC heatmap (every (train, test) pair on the truthfulness benchmarks) is mirrored almost entry-for-entry by the MCS heatmap. See Fig. 4, 5 and Tab. 2 in App. C for the generalization performance, MCS and ECS plotted against AUROC, and robustness to Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} estimators (full sample, Ledoit–Wolf, and per-coordinate diagonal) across all conditions.

3 Theory

3.1 Setup

Let X∈ℝdX\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a feature vector and Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\} a binary label. We analyse the OOD behaviour of a fixed direction widw_{\mathrm{id}}.

Assumption 1 (Moments).

Under the OOD distribution, Pr⁡(Y=0)=Pr⁡(Y=1)=12\Pr(Y{=}0){=}\Pr(Y{=}1){=}\tfrac{1}{2}, and the class-conditional distributions have means μ0,μ1\mu_{0},\mu_{1} and covariances Σ0,Σ1≻0\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1}\succ 0. Define δ≔μ1−μ0\delta\coloneqq\mu_{1}{-}\mu_{0} and Σpool≔12​(Σ0+Σ1)\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{2}(\Sigma_{0}{+}\Sigma_{1}).

Assumption 2 (Projection Gaussianity).

For each direction ww used in an AUROC statement below, the projection w⊤​X|Y=cw^{\top}X\mid Y{=}c is Gaussian for c∈{0,1}c\in\{0,1\}. This is much weaker than joint Gaussianity of XX, and plausible even for non-Gaussian distributions in a high dimensional space by projection concentration (a Diaconis–Freedman-style CLT for one-dimensional projections).

Empirically, the per-class projections are largely normal (Fig. 7), and simulations show the linearity survives clearly non-Gaussian projections (Fig. 8). Since the empirical projections are Gaussian, we retain this assumption for simplicity.

For w∈ℝd∖{0}w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\} we define

SNR⁡(w)≔w⊤​δw⊤​Σpool​w,zmax≔δ⊤​Σpool−1​δ,\SNR(w)\coloneqq\frac{w^{\top}\delta}{\sqrt{w^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}w}},z_{\max}\coloneqq\sqrt{\delta^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}^{-1}\delta}, (2)

In this section, woodw_{\mathrm{ood}} denotes the Fisher discriminant direction wood≔Σpool−1​δw_{\mathrm{ood}}{\coloneqq}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}^{-1}\delta, and we use s≔SNR⁡(wid)s{\coloneqq}\SNR(w_{\mathrm{id}}). In experiments, we substitute the OOD-trained logistic-regression direction for the Fisher discriminant direction. Empirically, MCS⁡(wid,woodLR)≈MCS⁡(wid,woodLDA)\MC(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}}){\approx}\MC(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}) in all settings (see Fig. 10 in App. I), and the R2R^{2} with AUROC are very close (see Tab. 2 in App. C), so the substitution is largely harmless.

3.2 Background results

The proof rests on three classic facts. We state them here and defer the textbook proofs to App. E.

Lemma 1 (Covariance decomposition).

Under Assumption 1, Σtot≔Cov⁡(X)=Σpool+14​δ​δ⊤\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}\coloneqq\Cov(X)=\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}+\tfrac{1}{4}\delta\delta^{\top}.

Lemma 2 (Binormal AUROC).

Under Assumptions 1–2, AUROC⁡(w)=Φ⁡(SNR⁡(w)/2)\AUROC(w){=}\Phi\!\bigl(\SNR(w)/\sqrt{2}\bigr), where Φ\Phi is the standard Gaussian CDF, for any w≠0w{\neq}0.

Lemma 3 (Fisher’s discriminant).

Under Assumption 1, SNR2⁡(w)\SNR^{2}(w) is maximised on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\} by any nonzero scalar multiple of wood=Σpool−1​δw_{\mathrm{ood}}=\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}^{-1}\delta, with maximum SNR zmax2=δ⊤​Σpool−1​δz_{\max}^{2}=\delta^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}^{-1}\delta, where zmaxz_{\max} is known as the Fisher distance.

3.3 Closed form for the Mahalanobis cosine

The Mahalanobis cosine of an arbitrary direction widw_{\mathrm{id}} with the Fisher direction woodw_{\mathrm{ood}} admits a closed form in two scalars: the SNR of widw_{\mathrm{id}} and the Fisher distance zmaxz_{\max} of the task.

Theorem 1 (Closed form for MCSΣtot\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}).

Under Assumption 1, for any widw_{\mathrm{id}} with wid⊤​Σpool​wid>0w_{\mathrm{id}}^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}w_{\mathrm{id}}>0 and zmax>0z_{\max}>0,

MCSΣtot⁡(wid,wood)=szmax​1+14​zmax21+14​s2,\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}})=\frac{s}{z_{\max}}\sqrt{\frac{1+\tfrac{1}{4}z_{\max}^{2}}{1+\tfrac{1}{4}s^{2}}}, (3)

where s≔SNR⁡(wid)s\coloneqq\SNR(w_{\mathrm{id}}). Moreover, in the large-Fisher-distance limit,

limzmax→∞MCSΣtot⁡(s)=s4+s2,\lim_{z_{\max}\to\infty}\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(s)\;=\;\frac{s}{\sqrt{4+s^{2}}}, (4)

the softsign function: bounded in (−1,1)(-1,1), nearly linear near s=0s{=}0, and saturating to ±1\pm 1 as |s|→∞|s|\to\infty.

The proof is a direct computation of the three quadratic forms in (1) using Lemma 1 (App. F). Although the derivation uses no objects beyond those already in the LDA literature, the resulting identity has not been written down, likely because the question it answers — how MCS of an arbitrary direction with the Fisher direction depends on SNR — was not previously connected to probe transfer.

The algebra is basic; what matters is the shape. On (−zmax,zmax)(-z_{\max},z_{\max}), MCSΣtot⁡(s)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(s) is odd, strictly increasing, and satisfies MCSΣtot⁡(±zmax)=±1\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(\pm z_{\max}){=}\pm 1. As zmax→∞z_{\max}{\to}\infty, MCSΣtot⁡(s)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(s) is exactly a softsign shape (Eq. 4; Fig. 2(b)).

3.4 Why AUROC is linear in MCS, with task-independent slope

Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 together imply that for a fixed OOD task (fixed zmaxz_{\max}), both AUROC\AUROC and MCSΣtot\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}} are monotone functions of the signal-to-noise ratio ss, tracing a parametric curve indexed only by zmaxz_{\max}. Two facts make this curve a near-linear law with a universal slope.

(i) Fixed zmaxz_{\max}: saturations cancel.

Differentiating the parametric curve at any ss gives:

d​AUROCd​MCSΣtot=ϕ⁡(s/2)​(1+s2/4)3/22/zmax2+1/2,\frac{d\,\AUROC}{d\,\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}}\;=\;\frac{\phi(s/\sqrt{2})\,(1+s^{2}/4)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2/z_{\max}^{2}+1/2}}, (5)

where ϕ\phi is the standard Gaussian density (App. G). The two ss-dependent factors are opposed in |s||s|: as |s||s| grows, ϕ⁡(s/2)\phi(s/\sqrt{2}) shrinks (the AUROC sigmoid saturating) while (1+s2/4)3/2(1{+}s^{2}/4)^{3/2} grows (the MCS softsign saturating). Their product is therefore much flatter than either factor alone, so the local slope stays close to its central value over the bulk of MCSΣtot∈(−1,1)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}\in(-1,1), as shown in Fig. 2c.

The cancellation is not exact: as |MCSΣtot|→1|\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}|\to 1, the Gaussian factor decays faster than the polynomial grows, and the local slope drops toward 00 (both data and theory at top-right of Fig. 2c flatten).

(ii) Per-task slope is universal.

The slope in Eq. 5 factors as h⁡(s)⋅g⁡(zmax)h(s)\cdot g(z_{\max}), where h⁡(s)h(s) captures ss-dependence and g⁡(zmax)=1/2/zmax2+1/2g(z_{\max}){=}1/\sqrt{2/z_{\max}^{2}+1/2} captures task dependence. At zmax>20z_{\max}{>}20, which holds in all empirical conditions (Tab. 3), g⁡(zmax)g(z_{\max}) lies within 0.5% of its limit. Therefore, the per-task AUROC–MCS curve aligns with the zmax→∞z_{\max}{\to}\infty limit curve to within 0.5%. At s=0s{=}0, this limit curve has central slope h⁡(0)⋅g⁡(∞)=1/πh(0)\cdot g(\infty){=}1/\sqrt{\pi} (App. G). Combined with (i), which establishes that the limit curve is approximately linear, with empirical slopes lying slightly below 1/π1/\sqrt{\pi} as expected (Fig. 9; App. G), since saturation-tail sampling drags the global slope down from its central value.

4 When does the linearity break down

The AUROC–MCS linearity holds when: MCS is computed against Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}, not Σpool\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}; the Fisher distance zmaxz_{\max} is large; class proportions are roughly balanced; the OOD probes are close to the optimal Fisher direction. Each ingredient can fail in practice. Fig. 3 shows what each violation does to the linearity; the four cases are quoted at the same axes throughout, and reported R2R^{2} are linear fits of OOD AUROC against MCS\MC.

(a) Wrong covariance. Using Σpool\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}} instead of Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} turns MCS\MC into s/zmaxs/z_{\max} exactly, so AUROC becomes a sigmoid in MCS rather than a line (see App. H for derivation). On the main experiment data, the linear fit R2R^{2} drops from 0.98 to 0.83.

(b) Non-Fisher probe. The theory does not hold if OOD probes deviate too much from the optimal Fisher directions, for example, for the commonly used difference of means probe Marks and Tegmark (2023). On the same empirical data, the diffmean probe gives a markedly lower R2R^{2} of 0.79. This delimits the law: it predicts generalization for Fisher-style probes (LR, LDA, shrinkage variants), not for diffmean-style probes.

(c) Small Fisher distance. For small zmaxz_{\max}, the slope of the MCS formula does not saturate, so each task is in its own near-linear regime with its own slope. Synthetic Gaussian data at zmax∈{0.1,0.5,1,2}z_{\max}\in\{0.1,0.5,1,2\} exhibits a clear fan of per-group slopes spanning a large range. The LLM data is unaffected because zmax>20z_{\max}{>}20 on every tasks (see Tab. 3; App. C). The linear fit is tight for each group, but taken together, the R2R^{2} drops to 0.666.

(d) Class imbalance. The balanced-class factor 14\tfrac{1}{4} in the MCS formula generalises to π⁡(1−π)\pi(1-\pi), so the AUROC–MCS slope steepens as π\pi moves away from 12\tfrac{1}{2} (App. H). Synthetic data at π∈{0.5,0.1,0.02,0.004}\pi\in\{0.5,0.1,0.02,0.004\} shows monotone steepening. The R2R^{2} drops to 0.84 in this case.

5 Discussion

Our results suggest that Mahalanobis cosine similarity is a theoretically sound alternative to standard Euclidean cosine similarity (consistent with recent arguments for non-Euclidean inner products (Park et al., 2024)). This also points to a broader research direction: many interpretability methods that currently rely on cosine similarity may benefit from the Mahalanobis alternative (steering-vector comparison, SAE feature alignment, concept-direction clustering, data filtering, data attribution, etc.). Future work can use unsupervised methods like CCS (Burns et al., 2023) for the OOD direction, enabling fully label-free prediction of probe generalization.

Limitations

Our results have several limitations. First, computing MCΣtot\mathrm{MC}_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}} requires estimating woodw_{\mathrm{ood}} and Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} from labeled OOD data; the method is training-free for the candidate probe widw_{\mathrm{id}} but not label-free for the target distribution. Second, the theory is calibrated to Fisher-style probes (LR, LDA); for difference-of-means probes the linearity degrades markedly (Fig. 3b), and a closed form for non-Fisher references remains open. Third, our evaluation is confined to binary classification on residual-stream features of autoregressive LLMs; multiclass probes, attention/MLP features, and non-LLM architectures are untested. Fourth, the law is fundamentally approximate: the per-task total slope is close to 1/π1/\sqrt{\pi} and the local slope goes to 0 at the extreme. Finally, the theory assumes per-class projection Gaussianity; while this holds empirically for most directions (Fig. 7) and the linearity survives clear violations in simulation (Fig. 8), formal guarantees do not extend to heavy-tailed projections.

Risks.

We do not foresee risks specific to this work; it is a theoretical analysis of an existing similarity measure.

Appendix A Extended related works

Linear probes and their generalization.

Linear probes are a standard interpretability tool (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Belinkov, 2022), used to read off concepts such as truthfulness (Marks and Tegmark, 2023), but often degrade under distribution shift (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Levinstein and Herrmann, 2024; Orgad et al., 2025). Prior work predicts linear-classifier generalization from geometric properties of the representation—kernel-target alignment (Cristianini et al., 2001), spectral rank (Garrido et al., 2023), and neural-collapse statistics (Papyan et al., 2020; Galanti et al., 2021)—but these score whole representations rather than individual probe directions. The near-linear AUROC–MCS relationship we explain was reported empirically by Ying et al. (2026) on truthfulness datasets; we prove it, characterize when it fails, and verify it across models, layers, and domains.

Classical statistical machinery.

Our theory composes three textbook results: Fisher’s linear discriminant (Fisher, 1936), the binormal AUROC formula (Bamber, 1975; Green et al., 1966; Hanley and McNeil, 1982), and the within–between covariance decomposition underlying MANOVA (Wilks, 1932; Chatfield, 2018). None is novel in isolation; the contribution lies in composing them into a closed-form quantity computable from a candidate probe direction together with two target-task moments.

Agreement-on-the-Line.

The closest theoretical neighbor is the Agreement-on-the-Line framework (Miller et al., 2021; Baek et al., 2022; Baek et al., 2025), which proves a linear ID-to-OOD relationship for probit-scaled accuracy and agreement rates between linear classifiers under Gaussian data. Baek et al. (2025) parameterize this relationship by a similarity that is algebraically the Mahalanobis cosine of Eq. (1). We differ in (i) targeting threshold-free AUROC, which admits the closed form of Theorem 1; (ii) predicting OOD performance from a single geometric quantity against the OOD Fisher direction, with no ID baseline; and (iii) identifying the universal slope around 1/π1/\sqrt{\pi} from the AUROC–MCS saturation cancellation, which has no analog in the AOL line.

Mahalanobis cosine as a similarity for direction comparison.

The most direct precursor of our setup is Bolme et al. (2003), who introduced "Mahalanobis cosine" as a similarity measure in PCA-whitened face-recognition pipelines. Iacovacci et al. (2020) reused the same expression for inferring omics networks. Both works treat MCS as a similarity score to be evaluated empirically against task performance; neither expresses MCS in closed form as a function of probe SNR and task Fisher distance, and neither links it to AUROC. Our contribution in §3 is to make precise why MCS works as a direction-comparison similarity for classification — in a closed form (Theorem 1) whose composition with the binormal AUROC is task-calibrated and predicts held-out performance.

Non-Euclidean geometry of LLM representations.

Park et al. (2024) also argue against Euclidean cosine on LLM representation space and propose a "causal inner product" derived from counterfactual considerations on the unembedding space. Their specific instantiation whitens by the covariance of unembedding token vectors, a single global matrix per model. Our Σt​o​t\Sigma_{tot} is a per-task activation covariance computed on the OOD train data, and operates in the residual-stream embedding space rather than the unembedding space.

Mahalanobis distance in OOD detection and transferability.

Mahalanobis distances of test points are widely used as out-of-distribution scores (Lee et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2021), but they score raw inputs rather than candidate probe directions. A separate transferability-metrics literature (LEEP, LogME, H-score, GBC, NCTI, Task2Vec; e.g. You et al., 2021; Pándy et al., 2022) predicts downstream linear-probe performance from frozen features, but operates on whole representations and typically requires target-side labels. To our knowledge, no prior method predicts the held-out AUROC of a specific probe direction in closed form from two target-task moments.

Appendix B Experimental details

B.1 Computational resources.

All experiments are done on local L40S and A40. Experiments require 4 GPUs to run for about 10 hours. We use Huggingface and NNsight to extract activations Wolf et al. (2020); Fiotto-Kaufman et al. (2024). The logistic regression probe is implemented with Pedregosa et al. (2011).

B.2 Model and probe details

Models.

We use Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B Grattafiori et al. (2024); Qwen et al. (2025). We use layer 15 and layer 19 for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B following Ying et al. (2026).

B.3 Dataset details

Truthfulness datasets.

We use ten total truthfulness datasets: five fundamental truth types from the FLEED dataset (definitional, empirical, logical, fictional, and ethical truth) (≈\approx8k samples), sycophantic lying (≈\approx4k samples), expectation inverted lying (≈\approx600 sample), and three on-policy deception datasets (roleplay (371 samples), insider trading (1.5k samples), and sandbagging (1k samples)) Scheurer et al. (2023); Benton et al. (2024); Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025); Ying et al. (2026). For Qwen-2.5-7B, we don’t have the three on-policy deception datasets. Therefore, it is evaluated only on 7 datasets.

Gender classification datasets.

We use six gender classification datasets: PAN17 Martinc et al. (2017), CrowdFlower Twitter gender classification Eight (2016), HappyDB Asai et al. (2018), BiosBias De-Arteaga et al. (2019), WinoBias Zhao et al. (2018), and GAP Webster et al. (2018). For datasets larger than 4000 samples, we randomly subsample to 4000 samples. Therefore, GAP has 2,000 samples, PAN17 randomly combines NN tweets from the same user and has 2,400 samples, WinoBias has 1,584 samples, and the rest has 4,000 samples each.

General NLP benchmarks.

We use eight classic NLP QA datasets: sentiment classification (IMDB Maas et al. (2011) and Amazon McAuley and Leskovec (2013)), topic classification (AG-News Zhang et al. (2015) and DBpedia-14 Lehmann et al. (2015)), NLI (RTE Wang et al. (2018)), question answering (BoolQ Clark et al. (2019)), and common sense reasoning Bisk et al. (2020)). We also subsample large datasets to 4,000 samples. Therefore, PIQA has 3,674 samples, RTE has 552 samples, and the rest has 4,000 samples each.

License.

All datasets used in this work are publicly available and applied here only for non-commercial academic evaluation, consistent with the terms set by their original authors. Explicit licenses, where available, are: MIT De-Arteaga et al. (2019); Zhao et al. (2018), Apache 2.0 Webster et al. (2018), CC BY-SA 3.0 Lehmann et al. (2015); Clark et al. (2019), Academic Free License v3.0 Bisk et al. (2020), and CC BY 4.0 Eight (2016); Scheurer et al. (2023). The remaining datasets are released under research-use terms specified in their associated publications. All data is English-language.

Appendix C Additional empirical results

Cross-domain generalization performance.

As shown in Fig 4, we observe rich cross-domain generalization patterns across all eight conditions.

MCS and ECS against AUROC.

Tab. 1 summarizes the performance of MCS and ECS on predicting OOD AUROC. We show the scatter plots for all eight conditions in Fig 5. We observe right cross-domain generalization patterns across all eight conditions.

Verification of the theory across conditions.

We show the theory against empirical data across all eight conditions in Fig. 6. In all conditions, the theoretical prediction tracks the empirical data very well.

Using wo​o​dL​D​Aw_{ood}^{LDA} instead of wo​o​dL​Rw_{ood}^{LR} for the empirical results.

We show the performance of using MCSΣtot⁡(wid,woodLR)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}}) vs. MCSΣtot⁡(wid,woodLDA)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}) to predict the OOD generalization performance in Tab. 2. Using MCSΣtot⁡(wid,woodLDA)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}) is better than MCSΣtot⁡(wid,woodLR)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}}) in all conditions, as expected. But the difference is small (<0.05<0.05).

Empirical AUROC–MCS slopes are consistent with theory.

As shown in Fig. 9, the empirically fitted slopes across 8 conditions are consistent with the theoretical prediction from App. G.

Measuring Gaussianity of the empirical data.

As shown in Fig. 7, most of the empirical skewness and kurtosis are small across all conditions, all probe directions, and all test data distributions. Specifically, 73% of the skewness is within ±0.5\pm 0.5 and 79% of the kurtosis is within ±1\pm 1.

Simulating non-Gaussian distributions.

As shown in Fig. 8, the AUROC–MCS R2R^{2} is extremely high in simulations, even for distributions that are deliberately designed to violate the projection-Gaussianity assumption.

Empirical zmaxz_{\max} across all datasets.

As shown in Tab. 3, all zmaxz_{\max} across all conditions and datasets exceed the saturation threshold zmax≥20z_{\max}\geq 20 at which the slopes lie within 0.5% of their limits (App. G), pinning all per-task AUROC–MCS slopes to a universal slope. The average zmaxz_{\max} for each condition is greater than 100, far exceeding the saturation point.

Robustness to the Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} estimator.

Tab. 2 reports the AUROC–-MCS linear-fit R2R^{2} under three estimators of Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}: the full sample covariance, Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage, and a per-coordinate diagonal approximation. Ledoit–Wolf is essentially indistinguishable from the full covariance across all conditions, so the headline result is not an artifact of a particular regularization choice. The diagonal approximation, by contrast, degrades sharply: most strikingly on general NLP (R2R^{2}=0.002 vs. 0.936), confirming that off-diagonal covariance structure is essential to MCS and that the linearity is not recoverable from per-coordinate variances alone.

From Lemma 2, AUROC⁡(s)=Φ⁡(s/2)\AUROC(s)=\Phi(s/\sqrt{2}), so d​AUROC/d​s=ϕ⁡(s/2)/2d\AUROC/ds=\phi(s/\sqrt{2})/\sqrt{2}. Combining with (7),

d​AUROCd​MCSΣtot\displaystyle\frac{d\AUROC}{d\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}} =d​AUROC/d​sg′​(s)\displaystyle=\frac{d\AUROC/ds}{g^{\prime}(s)}
=ϕ⁡(s/2)/2(1+α/zmax)(1+s2/4)−3/2,\displaystyle=\frac{\phi(s/\sqrt{2})/\sqrt{2}}{(\sqrt{1+\alpha}/z_{\max})(1+s^{2}/4)^{-3/2}},

which simplifies to (5).

Factorization into task and shape factors.

The slope (5) factors as

d​AUROCd​MCSΣtot=h⁡(s)⋅g⁡(zmax),\frac{d\AUROC}{d\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}}\;=\;h(s)\cdot g(z_{\max}),

where h⁡(s)=ϕ⁡(s/2)​(1+s2/4)3/2h(s)=\phi(s/\sqrt{2})\,(1+s^{2}/4)^{3/2} depends only on ss (task-independent), and g⁡(zmax)=1/2/zmax2+1/2g(z_{\max})=1/\sqrt{2/z_{\max}^{2}+1/2} depends only on zmaxz_{\max} (independent of ss). This decouples the two questions of (i) how flat the curve is within a task and (ii) how much the curve varies across tasks.

gg is strictly increasing in zmaxz_{\max} with limit g⁡(∞)=2g(\infty)=\sqrt{2}. Writing g⁡(zmax)/g⁡(∞)=1/1+4/zmax2g(z_{\max})/g(\infty)=1/\sqrt{1+4/z_{\max}^{2}}, the deviation from the limit is at most 0.5%0.5\% for zmax≥20z_{\max}\geq 20 and falls off as zmax−2z_{\max}^{-2}:

zmax46820g⁡(zmax)/g⁡(∞)0.8940.9490.9700.995\begin{array}[]{c|cccc}z_{\max}&4&6&8&20\\ \hline\cr g(z_{\max})/g(\infty)&0.894&0.949&0.970&0.995\end{array}

Shape factor h⁡(s)h(s) and central slope.

h⁡(s)h(s) combines ϕ⁡(s/2)\phi(s/\sqrt{2}) (strictly decreasing in |s||s|) with (1+s2/4)3/2(1+s^{2}/4)^{3/2} (strictly increasing in |s||s|). Their product is far flatter than either factor alone — this is the saturation cancellation behind (i): as |s|→zmax|s|\to z_{\max}, the AUROC sigmoid saturates (shrinking ϕ\phi) at the same time as the MCS softsign saturates (growing (1+s2/4)3/2(1+s^{2}/4)^{3/2}), and the two effects largely offset. The cancellation is not exact: h⁡(s)⋅g⁡(∞)h(s)\cdot g(\infty) peaks at s=±2s=\pm\sqrt{2} with value ≈0.629{\approx}0.629, then decays toward 00 as |s|→zmax|s|\to z_{\max}, which is why R2<1R^{2}<1 in the empirical AUROC–MCS fits.

Empirical slopes are consistent with theory.

As shown in Fig. 9, the empirically fitted slopes across 8 conditions are consistent with the theoretical prediction.

Appendix H Failure mode details

This appendix collects the formal statements behind the failure modes summarised in §4.

H.1 Use Σpool\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}} metric instead of Σtot\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}

We have:

wid⊤​Σpool​wood=wid⊤​δ=s​v;wid⊤​Σpool​wid=vw_{\mathrm{id}}^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}w_{\mathrm{ood}}=w_{\mathrm{id}}^{\top}\delta=s\sqrt{v};\ \ w_{\mathrm{id}}^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}w_{\mathrm{id}}=v

and

wood⊤​Σpool​wood=δ⊤​Σpool−1​δ=zmax2w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}w_{\mathrm{ood}}=\delta^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}^{-1}\delta=z_{\max}^{2}

Substituting into (1) gives s​v/(v⋅zmax)=s/zmaxs\sqrt{v}/(\sqrt{v}\cdot z_{\max})=s/z_{\max}. Therefore, MCSΣpool\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}} is just a rescaled ss. This will not cancel out the S-shaped between OOD AUROC and ss, and thus will not be linear to OOD AUROC.

∎

H.2 Small Fisher distance

When zmaxz_{\max} is small (zmax≲2z_{\max}\lesssim 2), the slope around 0 κ⁡(zmax)\kappa(z_{\max}) is far below its limit and varies rapidly with zmaxz_{\max}: κ⁡(1)≈0.25\kappa(1)\approx 0.25 vs. κ⁡(2)≈0.40\kappa(2)\approx 0.40 vs. κ⁡(3)≈0.47\kappa(3)\approx 0.47. A collection of test sets with heterogeneous small-zmaxz_{\max} tasks therefore does not collapse onto a single linear fit; each task has its own slope, producing a fan rather than a line. On synthetic data with zmaxz_{\max} controlled to {0.1,0.5,1,2}\{0.1,0.5,1,2\} (Fig. 3c), we observe exactly this fan, and the global linear R2R^{2} drops to 0.666. This failure mode is not engaged on our LLM datasets because every task has zmax>20z_{\max}>20, inside the saturation regime (see Tab. 3; App. C).

H.3 Strong class imbalance

For class prior π\pi, we redefine the pooled vvariance as:

Σpool≔(1−π)​Σ0+π​Σ1\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}\coloneqq(1-\pi)\Sigma_{0}+\pi\Sigma_{1}

Then Lemma 1 generalises to

Σtot=Σpool+π⁡(1−π)​δ​δ⊤\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}+\pi(1-\pi)\,\delta\delta^{\top}

, and Theorem 1 becomes

MCSΣtot⁡(wid,wood)=szmax​1+π⁡(1−π)​zmax21+π⁡(1−π)​s2,\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}){=}\frac{s}{z_{\max}}\sqrt{\frac{1+\pi(1-\pi)z_{\max}^{2}}{1+\pi(1-\pi)s^{2}}},

preserving the softsign-cancels-sigmoid story but with a re-scaled saturation point and slope. Strong imbalance (e.g., π=0.01\pi=0.01) shrinks the π⁡(1−π)\pi(1-\pi) factor by 25×25\times versus the balanced case, weakening the saturation cancellation in MCS and steepening the AUROC–MCS slope. Our probe datasets are all approximately balanced, so this mode is not engaged in our experiments, but it would matter for naturally imbalanced applications such as rare-event detection.

Appendix I Empirical alignment of LR and LDA reference directions

The theory in §3 uses the Fisher direction woodLDA=Σpool−1​δw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}=\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}^{-1}\delta as the OOD reference. In the empirical experiments, we replace it with the OOD-trained logistic-regression direction woodLRw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}}, on the grounds that for balanced binary tasks with well-separated classes the two directions are nearly proportional. This appendix quantifies the substitution.

Setup.

For each of datasets used in §2, on the train half of a stratified 50/50 split, we compute (i) the Fisher direction woodLDA=(Σpool+λ​I)−1​δw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}=(\Sigma_{\mathrm{pool}}+\lambda I)^{-1}\delta with λ=10−6\lambda=10^{-6}, and (ii) the LR direction woodLRw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}}. We measure the correlation between MC(wi​dL​Rw^{LR}_{id}, wo​o​dL​Rw^{LR}_{ood}) and MC(wi​dL​Rw^{LR}_{id}, wo​o​dL​D​Aw^{LDA}_{ood}).

Result.

As shown in Fig. 10, across all settings (across models, layers, and concept domains), the pairwise Pearson correlation between MCSΣtot⁡(wid,woodLR)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}}) and MCSΣtot⁡(wid,woodLDA)\MC_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}}(w_{\mathrm{id}},w_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}) is r>0.99r>0.99, with mean |Δ⁡(wid)|<0.07|\Delta(w_{\mathrm{id}})|<0.07. Substituting woodLRw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}} for woodLDAw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}} in the headline regression of §2 changes the linear-fit R2R^{2} by less than 1%.

Why this works.

For balanced binary classification with classes that are jointly well-modelled by Gaussians with shared covariance, the LR maximum-likelihood direction and the Fisher direction coincide up to scaling Efron (1975); Hastie (2009). Real activations only approximately satisfy these assumptions, but all of our probe datasets are easy — ID AUROC exceeds 0.950.95 in every case — so the residual mismatch between woodLRw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LR}} and woodLDAw_{\mathrm{ood}}^{\mathrm{LDA}} is small in cosine. We expect a larger mismatch on harder, less-separable tasks; characterising that regime is a useful direction for future work.
